headline: Two dead and up to 20 unaccounted for after flash flooding in the inner Grand Canyon
dek: A wall of water came down Bright Angel Creek on Saturday afternoon, destroying nearly all the footbridges along it and forcing the airlift of 62 people from Phantom Ranch. The National Park Service has given several different figures for the number of people unaccounted for.
summary: Flash flooding along Bright Angel Creek in the Grand Canyon has killed two people and left as many as 20 unaccounted for, the National Park Service says. Sixty-two people were airlifted out of the inner canyon.

queries: muddy floodwater in a dry wash
image.alt: A deep desert canyon with sheer rock walls and a silt-brown river running along its floor

body.text: Two people have died and as many as twenty are unaccounted for after flash flooding tore down Bright Angel Creek on the floor of the Grand Canyon on Saturday afternoon, the United States National Park Service said. Sixty-two people were airlifted out of Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail, and the inner canyon's water pipeline and nearly all of the footbridges over the creek were destroyed. The search was continuing on Monday.

Bright Angel Creek runs from the canyon's North Rim down to the Colorado River, and Phantom Ranch sits at the bottom of it — a cluster of cabins and a campground reachable only on foot, by mule or by raft. The flooding began in Bright Angel Canyon at about 2:30pm on Saturday, according to Fox Weather. Heavy rain had fallen through the afternoon.

The number of people unaccounted for changed repeatedly through Monday, and the Park Service has been careful to describe them as unaccounted for rather than as confirmed missing — a distinction that matters in a place with almost no mobile telephone coverage. Reuters, in a dispatch carried by The Spokesman-Review, reported the Park Service as saying more than twenty people were potentially missing or unaccounted for. ABC News, publishing on Monday evening, gave at least fourteen on the same authority. CBS News, reporting early on Monday morning, said the Park Service believed around fifteen people were still missing. Fox Weather described the figure as more than a dozen. This wire could not establish a single reconciled number.

The death toll moved in the same way. CBS News, reporting on Monday morning, said one body had been recovered on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids on the Colorado River. Reuters and ABC News, both later on Monday, put the number of confirmed deaths at two. Neither of the two people who died is named here, and no identifying detail about them appears in this article.
The rain, and the ground it fell on

The National Weather Service recorded four separate rounds of rain over roughly six hours on Saturday, according to ABC News. The first three were light. The fourth was torrential, and it fell on ground that could not take it. Two factors made the runoff worse, the weather service said: the steepness of the canyon itself, and the burn scar left on the North Rim by the Dragon Bravo Fire, where vegetation that would normally slow water is gone. That attribution comes from the weather service by way of ABC News; the Fox Weather account of the same event does not mention the burn scar.
Most of it ran off instantly.
body.cite: Justin Johndrow, National Weather Service meteorologist in Flagstaff, via CBS News

body.text: Fox Weather's in-house forecasting unit put the rainfall at between one and one and three-quarter inches, and said gauges on the Colorado River had spiked by as much as nine feet. Those are the outlet's own measurements rather than a public authority's, and they are reported here as such. The same unit rated the flash flood threat for Monday at three out of four for parts of Utah and two out of four for northern Arizona. The National Weather Service kept a flood watch in place through at least Monday evening and warned that flash flooding from excessive rainfall remained possible across northern and central Arizona.

The damage below the rim is substantial. The Park Service said the flooding wrecked infrastructure in the inner canyon including the Transcanyon Waterline, the pipeline that carries drinking water to the canyon's developed areas and which has been the subject of a long replacement project. Crossings along the creek are gone.
Nearly all footbridges spanning Bright Angel Creek were destroyed, eliminating hiker access across the creek.
body.cite: National Park Service statement, via Fox Weather

body.text: Phantom Ranch, the Bright Angel Campground, the Phantom Ranch canteen, the North Kaibab Trail, the Black and Silver bridges and river traffic through the affected stretch of the Colorado are all closed until further notice, CBS News reported. The North Rim of the park was already closed for the season. There is no published estimate of how long the inner canyon will stay shut, or of what the repairs will cost.

The rescue itself worked. Sixty-two people were lifted out by helicopter from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail on Saturday and Sunday, and the Park Service has appealed for information from anyone who was in the inner canyon and has since made it out — which is part of why the figure for those unaccounted for has been falling as the days pass rather than climbing.

body.title: On the figures in this article
items: The number of people unaccounted for is provisional and was revised several times on Monday alone.
Where four outlets give four different figures from the same authority, all four are reported above.
Nobody who died, was rescued or is unaccounted for is named in this article.

uncertain: How many people are actually unaccounted for. Figures attributed to the National Park Service on Monday ranged from at least fourteen to more than twenty, and the sources read do not agree on a single number or explain the differences.

Whether the confirmed death toll of two supersedes the single recovery reported on Monday morning, or whether a second body was found later in the day. The sources read do not say when or where the second death was confirmed.
How many people were in the inner canyon when the flooding began. No total was published by the Park Service in any account read.
Whether the burn scar from the Dragon Bravo Fire contributed to the runoff. This is attributed to the National Weather Service by ABC News and is not mentioned in the other accounts read.

The rainfall totals and river-gauge rise, which come from Fox Weather's own forecasting unit rather than from the National Weather Service, and which this wire could not corroborate against a public authority's measurement.
How long the inner canyon and the affected trails will remain closed, and the cost or timescale of repairing the Transcanyon Waterline and the destroyed footbridges.
Whether the two people who died were park visitors, staff or river users. This was not established from the sources read, and no identifying detail is reported here in any case.
